teaser.text: MTR Corporation Limited is a railway company whose business reaches beyond trains: it earns from fares, property, rents and services built around the network. To understand how a dollar moves through MTR, follow the journey from passenger and tenant payments to railway costs, property gains and the risks that shape each stream.

stock.opening: MTR's weighted forecast is HK$20.72 in October 2027 and HK$16.64 in October 2029; the bear case carries 25% probability, the base case 55%, and the bull case 20%. It hinges on whether property cash can fund railway growth without worsening cash conversion, debt or dividend pressure.
stock.closing: The full memo also explains MTR's business, rivals, management and risks.

paragraphs.text: The weighted forecast is HK$20.72 in October 2027, a -32% total return. It is HK$16.64 in October 2029, a -36% total return. The bear case carries 25% probability. The base case carries 55%, and the bull case 20%.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for MTR?

paragraphs.text: The bear case requires property weakness and funding pressure to persist together. Delayed completions or weak bids would reduce development profit, while frozen fares, negative rental reversion and construction costs would limit recurring growth. Net debt would rise as spending outpaces cash receipts, putting dividends and the multiple under pressure. The bear price is HK$12.80 at the first date and HK$0.18 at the last. Its 25% probability reflects negative free cash flow, negative transport EBIT and high planned expenditure, but recurring transport and rental income keep it below the specialists’ 30% downside odds.

The bull case requires timely property tenders, strong completions, firm ridership and disciplined spending. Those conditions would improve cash conversion, reduce funding risk and support a rerating alongside EBITDA growth. The bull price is HK$30.19 initially and HK$38.61 at the last date. Its 20% probability reflects the strength of the potential upside, but also the need for several favorable events to arrive together despite weak rental reversion and heavy investment needs.

blocks.heading: How much cash does MTR really make?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow is the cash left after operating cash flow, capital spending, lease payments and interest paid. These are analytical measures rather than MTR’s own profit lines. In 2025, operating cash flow was positive, but those outflows exceeded it. Real free cash flow goes further by subtracting stock-based pay, and it remained negative in every year of the five-year table.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for MTR today?

paragraphs.text: Accounting earnings also leave out an important cash need. A railway must replace trains, signalling systems, tracks and stations even when passenger revenue looks healthy. Free cash flow goes further than profit or EBITDA because it subtracts actual investment spending. MTR’s renewal and construction programme therefore matters more than a low earnings multiple alone.

dividend.title: MTR dividend history and cash coverage
dividend.meta_description: MTR paid HK$1.31 per share for 2025, while free cash flow was negative throughout the years shown.
dividend.opening: MTR paid an ordinary dividend of HK$1.31 per share for 2025 and has held that annual amount since 2022. Free cash flow was negative throughout the years shown, so operations did not generate enough surplus after investment to cover everything MTR paid out.
dividend.closing: The full MTR memo also answers how MTR runs its business, compares with rivals, assesses management, and weighs its risks.

blocks.heading: How much does MTR pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: The dividend path reflects policy constrained by cash needs. MTR paid HK$1.31 per share for 2025 and has held that annual amount since 2022. The base keeps the first forecast dividend at HK$1.31, then raises it by one cent at each later date. The bear case cuts to HK$1.25 and then HK$1.20. The bull case rises to HK$1.35 initially and HK$1.45 eventually. Five years of negative free cash flow and roughly HK$140 billion of committed railway investment make large increases difficult, despite the stated policy to maintain or steadily increase dividends.

blocks.heading: Is MTR's dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow means cash left after ordinary operations and capital investment. It was negative throughout the years shown. That does not mean MTR’s bank account was empty, because the company could also use cash balances, property receipts, borrowing and other financing. It does mean that operations did not generate enough surplus after investment to cover everything the company paid out.

MTR also continued paying dividends. Buybacks were much smaller and represented purchases for the Executive Share Incentive Scheme, not a separate large return-of-capital programme. Debt moved in both directions: MTR issued debt and repaid debt in every year shown. Borrowing therefore helped manage the timing gap between investment, shareholder distributions and cash generated in a particular year.

paragraphs.text: The coming 12 months will test whether property proceeds can support railway investment as projects move from tender to cash receipt. Fare recoupment in 2027/28 and transport results through 2027–2028 will show whether fares keep pace with operating costs. Cash conversion and net debt through 2028 and 2029 will test dividend resilience.

blocks.heading: What is MTR's dividend yield today?

paragraphs.text: A dividend yield is the annual dividend divided by the share price, not a promise of surplus cash. MTR paid an ordinary dividend of HK$1.31 per share for 2025, but it must first operate trains, renew assets, build lines and service debt. The Hong Kong SAR Government owns 74.45% of MTR, leaving a 25.55% free float, so the quoted market value applies to every share even though only a smaller portion trades freely.
